text:
AROUND TOWN
Billings events
WOODSTOCK — New this year, Billings Farm & Museum will be open from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. Friday through Monday, starting in March, with maple tastings, butter-making programs, and Saturday pop-up activities for young visitors and their caregivers. Visitors can also enjoy weekend horse-drawn sleigh rides, two exhibitions, catch the final three films of the Woodstock Vermont Film Series, and celebrate Maple Open House Weekend.
Films will be screened at 3 p.m. at Billings Farm & Museum Visitor Center Theater. Tickets are $15 for all regular screenings, $12 for Billings Farm & Museum members, at: billingsfarm.org/filmseries.
“Folktales” screening Saturday and Sunday, Feb. 28 and March 1. “Folktales” takes viewers on a journey to Arctic Norway, where teenagers spend a “gap year” at Pasvik Folk High School.
“Every Little Thing” screening Saturday and Sunday, March 14 and 15. “Every Little Thing” follows author and wildlife rehabilitator Terry Masear on her mission to rescue every injured hummingbird in Los Angeles.
“Natchez” screening Saturday and Sunday, March 21 and 22. “Natchez” shows the clash between history and memory in a small Mississippi town.
Maple Open House Weekend, 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. Saturday and Sunday, March 21 and 22. Guests view Vermont’s maple history and learn about maple syrup traditions.
Horse-drawn sleigh rides are offered from 11 a.m. to 3 p.m. March 7, 8, 15, 21 and 28, conditions permitting. Tickets are $5/person ages 2 and above, in addition to admission to Billings Farm & Museum. Tickets can be purchased at the admissions desk. Private sleigh rides are available for booking through March at: billingsfarm.org/horse-drawn-rides.
Winter carnival
POULTNEY — Poultney Valley Snowmobile Club will hold a winter carnival from 10:30 a.m. to 4 p.m. Saturday, Feb. 14, at Bob Chesnut’s home on York Street Extension. Open to the public, the event features free snowmobile rides, sliding, games and lunch foods. For more information, call 802-287-9755.
HEALTH
Cardiac arrest
More than 350,000 out-of-hospital cardiac arrests occur in the U.S. each year. Nine out of every 10 people who experience cardiac arrest outside of a hospital die, in part because they do not receive immediate CPR more than half of the time.
This February, during American Heart Month, the American Heart Association is calling on everyday citizens to step in as the first responder until professional help arrives.
1. Learn CPR. In Vermont, individuals and families can take an online or in-person CPR course, watch a 90-second video to learn Hands-Only CPR for adults or watch this video to learn how to save an infant or child using CPR with breaths. To learn more about CPR, visit: heart.org/nation.
2. Make a plan. During a cardiac emergency, a well-developed plan could make all the difference. Don’t wait for help, become it. A cardiac emergency response plan or (CERP) establishes specific steps to reduce death from cardiac arrest in any setting. Learn more about CERPs and find free resources at heart.org/cerp.
3. Get local. Join the Vermont Heart Walk, take a CPR class, or make sure your office, school or church has a plan.
AROUND VT
Red Bench series
STOWE — As part of the Vermont Ski and Snowboard Museum’s Red Bench Speaker Series, an evening of storytelling, cinematography and photography that ties together three generations of a Stowe family of filmmakers, will be held at 6:30 p.m. Thursday, Feb. 12, doors open at 6 p.m., at 1 South Main St., Stowe.
Lew and Freedle Coty tell how skiing and snowboarding have influenced their lives, with footage and pictures of feats and adventures of skiers and snowboarders. David Goodman, New York Times writer and author of backcountry ski guidebooks, will moderate the event, which will end with a Q&A session.
Event admission is $10 and can be purchased in advance at www.vtssm.org/new-events. Red Bench Speaker Series sponsors include rk Miles, Spruce Peak, and Sisler Builders.

Simply email the information to us at news@rutlandherald.com. Be sure to put For Community News in the subject line. (Note: We do reserve the right to edit for length.)
